# Lābhasakkāra Saṁyutta (SN 17)
**ID:** SN 17
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Lābhasakkāra Saṁyutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn17
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Lābhasakkārasaṁyutta* ("Linked Discourses on Gains and Honor") is the seventeenth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, comprising 43 suttas arranged into four chapters [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994]. The opening discourse is set in Sāvatthī at Jeta's Grove in Anāthapiṇḍika's Park [Bodhi 2003]. Throughout the saṁyutta, the Buddha warns mendicants against the grave spiritual dangers and corrupting enticements posed by material acquisition, favors, and renown (*lābhasakkārasiloka*) [SuttaCentral; Marino 2017; Pande 1974]. The commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*) glosses "gain" (*lābha*) as the acquisition of the four monastic requisites, "honor" (*sakkāra*) as the receipt of requisites that are well made and superior, and "praise" (*siloka*) as fame or acclamation [Bodhi 2003].
The collection is unified by a characteristic doctrinal refrain: "dreadful, bitter, and harsh are gains, honor, and praise, an obstacle to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage"—a formula that G. C. Pande suggests may represent an early core of the collection [Pande 1974]. Pedagogically, the text is noted for repeating its central warning multiple times through varied, vivid similes, including that of a fish enticed by a baited hook [Hazra 1994; Marino 2017]. In one well-known sutta (*Ekaputtakasutta*, SN 17.23), the Buddha outlines distinct models of emulation for his followers, stating that a mother should encourage a lay son to model himself upon the exemplary householders Citta and Hatthaka of Āḷavī, but to emulate Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna should he enter the monastic Sangha [Nyanaponika et al. 2003].
External parallels to suttas of the *Lābhasakkārasaṁyutta* are preserved primarily in the Chinese *Ekottarika-āgama* (e.g., EĀ 9.1, 9.2, 11.7–8, 12.9, 23.7, and 25.8), as well as in the *Saṁyukta-āgama* (SĀ 1064) and *Bieyi za ahan jing* (SA2 3) for discourses concerning Devadatta (SN 17.35–36) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates these cross-language alignments with the *Ekottarika-āgama* (T 125) and *Saṁyukta-āgama* (T 99), and further identifies significant shared textual material in the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* [DharmaNexus]. Textual material also corresponds closely with the Vinaya Piṭaka's *Saṁghabhedakakkhandhaka* (*Cullavagga* 7), where similes illustrating how gain brings self-destruction—such as the fruit that kills the bamboo, the reed, or the plantain—are shared between both texts [Perez-Remon 1980; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects substantial Pali-internal text reuse with the *Opamma Saṁyutta* (SN 20), *Dhātu Saṁyutta* (SN 14), and numerous nipātas of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* [DharmaNexus].
